content: Place cells are a specific type of principal neurons located in the hippocampus. These neurons exhibit a high frequency of firing when an animal is in a particular location within its environment, a region referred to as the cell's place field. Place cells are distinct from other spatially modulated neurons, such as grid cells, head direction cells, and spatial view cells. In the CA1 and CA3 subfields of the hippocampus, place cells are believed to be pyramidal cells, whereas in the dentate gyrus, they are thought to be granule cells. The concept of place cells was first described in rats by O'Keefe and Dostrovsky. Based on this discovery, O'Keefe and Nadel proposed that the primary function of the hippocampus in rats is to construct a cognitive map of their environment. Similar cells with analogous properties have been identified in the human hippocampus through extracellular recordings in epilepsy patients undergoing invasive brain activity monitoring. Place cells increase their firing rate significantly when an animal is within their specific place field. Outside this field, the firing rate is nearly zero, but within the center of the place field, it can reach up to 100 Hz for brief periods. When a rat moves randomly in an environment, the firing of place cells is generally not influenced by the direction the animal is facing. However, in tasks involving directed movement (e.g., shuttling between goal locations), place cells often fire in a direction-specific manner, being active only when the animal passes through the place field in a particular direction. Upon initial exposure to a new environment, place fields are established within minutes and remain stable across repeated exposures to the same environment. In a different environment, a place cell may exhibit a completely different place field or none at all, a phenomenon known as remapping. Approximately 40-50% of hippocampal place cells are active in any given environment. In environments with minimal directional cues, such as a circular space surrounded by black curtains, place fields tend to maintain a fixed radial position. However, the entire set of place fields may rotate around the maze, consistent with the theory that rats gradually lose their orientation. When a polarizing cue, such as a large white rectangle, is introduced, place fields align with fixed positions relative to the cue. If the cue is moved while the animal can see it, the place fields remain unaffected. However, if the animal is briefly removed from the environment, the cue is moved, and the animal is returned, the place fields rotate to maintain their alignment with the cue card. Although visual cues are the primary determinant of place cell firing, the persistence of firing in complete darkness suggests that other sensory inputs, such as proprioception, also contribute. In linear track environments, where a rat is constrained to move along a defined path, place fields often exhibit a directional component in addition to their spatial component. A place cell that fires at a specific location when the rat moves in one direction along the track may not fire when the rat visits the same location from the opposite direction. However, if the rat frequently turns around at a specific point, place fields at that location may become independent of direction. The size and signal-to-noise ratio of place fields vary depending on the hippocampal region. Place fields are smallest and most sharply defined at the dorsal pole of the hippocampus, becoming larger toward the ventral pole. This variation may reflect the topography of projections to the hippocampus. For instance, the ventral hippocampus receives substantial input from the amygdala, while the dorsal hippocampus is preferentially innervated by the entorhinal cortex. Spatially modulated cells are also found in the entorhinal cortex, which provides input from the neocortex to the hippocampus. Neurons in the lateral entorhinal cortex exhibit minimal spatial selectivity, whereas neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEA) display multiple place fields arranged in a hexagonal pattern, earning them the designation of grid cells. The size of these fields and the spacing between them increase progressively from the dorso-lateral MEA to the ventro-medial MEA. The hippocampus is one of several brain structures capable of generating a characteristic 4-12 Hz oscillation known as the theta rhythm, observable in EEG recordings. This oscillation has been documented across all tested mammalian species and is associated with real or virtual movement through space in both rats and humans. When a neuron fires, it does so in relation to the current phase of the theta cycle (0-360 degrees). As a rat enters a cell's place field, the cell initially fires when perisomatic inhibition is weakest, corresponding approximately to the peak of the theta oscillation recorded in the CA1 pyramidal cell layer. With each subsequent theta cycle, as the rat progresses through the place field, the cell fires at progressively earlier phases, typically ceasing just before the trough of the cycle. This phenomenon, known as phase precession, results in the place cell firing at a slightly higher frequency than the ongoing theta oscillation. Because the place fields of different cells overlap, at any given moment, the rat will be at varying distances within different fields. Consequently, each place cell fires at a distinct phase of the theta cycle, enabling the rat's position to be determined with high precision. This mechanism potentially provides an alternative temporal code for spatial location. Phase precession also compresses the temporal sequences of place cell firing, a phenomenon thought to facilitate synaptic plasticity. Evidence suggests that phase precession is related to the depolarization of the neuron, such that the firing rate and firing phase of the cell are tightly coupled. However, phase precession can also occur independently of firing rate in freely moving animals. This observation highlights the need for further investigation into the underlying neural mechanisms of phase precession before definitive conclusions can be drawn.
